title: The Last Lesson
author: Alphonse Daudet
tagline: Short story · told by a schoolboy · language, loss and love of one's country

overview.intro: A young schoolboy named Franz sets off for school one morning, dreading a scolding because he has not prepared his lesson. He finds the village strangely quiet and the classroom unusually solemn. His teacher, M. Hamel, is dressed in his best clothes, and villagers sit silently at the back. Franz learns that an order has come from Berlin: from tomorrow only German will be taught in the schools of Alsace. This is the last French lesson. The story shows how people often realise the worth of their language, their teachers and their opportunities only when they are about to lose them.

facts.label: Genre
facts.value: Short story; a tale of patriotism and language

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: A village school in Alsace, France, just after the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71), when the region passed under Prussian control

facts.label: Narrator
facts.value: Franz, a schoolboy, telling the story in the first person

facts.label: Main characters
facts.value: Franz, M. Hamel (the teacher), and the older villagers in the classroom

facts.label: Central concern
facts.value: The value of one's mother tongue and the danger of postponing what matters

learn.title: Before you read: the historical setting

blocks.text: France and Prussia fought a war in 1870-71, which France lost. Alsace, a border region, came under Prussian control. The new rulers decided that schools there should teach only German. Many people in the region spoke French at home and in school, so the order was felt as an attack on their identity.

The story is told through the eyes of a child. Franz does not understand politics at first, and the reader watches his understanding grow from a careless boy who wants to play truant to someone who feels the weight of the moment.

items: Franz is late for school and is tempted to skip school and spend the fine morning outdoors. He resists the temptation and hurries to school, afraid that M. Hamel will scold him for not knowing his lesson.
On the way he notices a small crowd near the village notice-board, where bad news has been posted in recent times. He has no time to stop.
Unusually, the school is calm. Normally there is noise and confusion; today the room is hushed. M. Hamel, usually strict, speaks to him gently and asks him to take his seat.
Franz then sees that his teacher is wearing his best clothes, normally kept for special occasions, and that elderly villagers are sitting at the back of the class, looking sad.

M. Hamel announces that an order has come from Berlin: only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace. This is the last French lesson. Franz is shocked and full of regret for all the lessons he wasted.

M. Hamel praises French as the clearest and most beautiful language in the world. He says the people must guard it among themselves, because a people that keeps its language holds the key to its freedom. He blames himself and the parents as well as the pupils for having put learning off.
The lesson continues with reading, writing and grammar. Even the old men at the back join in, spelling out letters like children. Franz listens with an attention he has never shown before.
When the church clock strikes noon, M. Hamel is too overcome to speak. He writes Vive la France on the blackboard and, with a gesture, dismisses the class.

items.meaning: A young, easily distracted schoolboy who begins as an unwilling learner. Over the course of one morning he becomes serious, ashamed of his neglect and deeply attached to his language and teacher. His change is the emotional centre of the story.

The village teacher, normally strict and impatient. On the last day he is gentle, dignified and full of regret. Wearing his best clothes shows respect for the occasion and for his pupils. He admits his own faults, and his final gesture shows his love of his country.

Older men, and others from the village, who sit at the back of the classroom. They had once neglected school themselves, and their presence is a mark of respect for the teacher and a sign of regret for lost opportunities.
A language carries a people's history, feelings and pride. When rulers forbid it, they threaten the community's sense of who it is.
Both children and adults put off learning, always assuming there would be time later. The loss of the chance shows them what they undervalued.
Patriotism in this story is quiet and personal, expressed in a final lesson and a few words on a blackboard, not in speeches or weapons.
What seemed a burden to Franz, such as books, grammar and a strict teacher, becomes precious the moment it is taken away.

blocks.text: Central idea: we often fail to value our language, our teachers and our chances until they are about to be taken from us, so we should not postpone learning or take freedom for granted.

items: First-person child narrator: the events are filtered through Franz's changing feelings, which makes the story simple, direct and emotional.
Contrast: the noisy, careless school of ordinary days is set against the silent, solemn last day. The contrast of Franz's morning mood and his mood at the end shows the change in him.
Symbolism: M. Hamel's best clothes symbolise respect and mourning; the villagers at the back symbolise the whole community's regret; the blackboard message is the teacher's act of defiance and love.
Irony: the people who neglected French for years now sit eagerly to learn it, when it is almost too late.
Pathos: the sadness comes from small, ordinary details, such as the teacher's emotion at the end, without any dramatic narration.
Foreshadowing: the crowd at the notice-board and the unusual quiet hint at the announcement before Franz understands them.

learn.title: How to use this story in an answer

items: Mention both the historical cause (the order from Berlin after the war) and the human effect (the changes in Franz and his teacher).
Do not present M. Hamel as only a hero. He also blames himself, which is what makes him believable.
For character answers, show change: say what Franz was at the start, what he becomes, and what causes the shift.
For theme questions, link language to identity and freedom, and link regret to postponing.
Refer to the ending: the message on the blackboard and the gesture of dismissal are strong evidence.

keyPoints: The story is narrated by Franz, a schoolboy in an Alsatian village after the Franco-Prussian War.
An order from Berlin permits only German to be taught, so this is the final French lesson.
M. Hamel wears his best clothes and old villagers sit at the back as a mark of respect and regret.
M. Hamel praises French, says a people who keep their language keep the key to their freedom, and blames himself as well as the parents.
Franz changes from a careless boy into a serious, regretful learner in a single morning.
The teacher ends by writing Vive la France on the board and dismissing the class by a gesture.
examFocus: Character sketch of M. Hamel and of Franz, showing change.
Why the story is called The Last Lesson and what is being lost.
The importance of a mother tongue and its link with freedom and identity.
The meaning of the villagers' presence at the back of the room.
Regret and postponement as a theme: who is to blame for the neglected lessons.
The significance of the ending and the words on the blackboard.

questions.prompt: What order had come from Berlin?
options: Only French was to be taught in schools
Only German was to be taught in the schools of Alsace
All village schools were to be closed
M. Hamel was to be dismissed and replaced by a new teacher
questions.answer: Only German was to be taught in the schools of Alsace.
questions.explanation: The order from the new rulers meant that French lessons would end, making this the last French lesson.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the schools were being shut. They were to continue, but in German.

questions.prompt: Why was Franz afraid to go to school that morning?
options: He had heard that the school would be closed
He was afraid the villagers would be angry
He had not prepared his lesson and expected a scolding from M. Hamel
He was ill and wanted to stay in bed
questions.answer: He had not prepared his lesson and expected a scolding from M. Hamel.
questions.explanation: Franz was late and unprepared, so he expected the usual strictness. Instead he found an unusually gentle teacher.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option about the school closing. Franz learns about the order only after reaching class.

questions.prompt: What does M. Hamel write on the blackboard at the end of the story?
options: The date of the last lesson
questions.explanation: Too moved to speak, the teacher writes these words as a last expression of love for his country.
questions.commonMistake: Believing he made a long speech at the end. He was unable to speak and used the board.

questions.prompt: What unusual things did Franz notice when he reached the classroom?
questions.answer: The room was hushed instead of noisy, M. Hamel was wearing his best clothes instead of his ordinary ones, and elderly villagers were sitting silently at the back of the class. These signs showed Franz that something serious was about to happen.
questions.explanation: Give at least two of the three changes and say what they suggest. The calm and the special clothes are clues before the announcement.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only the noise. The teacher's clothes and the villagers are equally important.

questions.prompt: Why were the old villagers sitting at the back of the classroom?
questions.answer: They had come to show respect for M. Hamel, who had taught for many years, and to express their gratitude and sorrow at the end of French teaching. Many also regretted that they had not learned enough when they were young, so they wished to attend this final lesson. Their presence shows that the whole community was affected by the loss.
questions.explanation: Cover respect for the teacher, regret about neglected learning, and the sense of a shared loss.
questions.commonMistake: Saying they had come to complain or to check on the children.

questions.prompt: What did M. Hamel say about the French language, and why was it important to him?
questions.answer: M. Hamel described French as a very clear, beautiful and logical language, the finest in the world. He urged the people to guard it among themselves and never forget it, since a people who keep their language hold something like the key to their captivity. For him the language was tied to identity and freedom, so losing it meant losing part of the self.
questions.explanation: State his praise, his advice to protect the language, and the link between language and freedom, all in your own words.
questions.commonMistake: Making it a simple praise of grammar. His point is about identity and freedom.

questions.prompt: How does Franz change during the course of the story? What causes this change?
questions.answer: At the start Franz is careless: he wants to escape school and spend the morning outside, and he has not learned his lesson. After he learns that this is the last French lesson, he feels shame and regret for his wasted time. The books that were a burden now seem like old friends, and even M. Hamel, whom he disliked for his strictness, seems different. By the end he listens with full attention and understands the value of the language and of his teacher. The change is caused by the sudden news that the opportunity is being taken away.
questions.explanation: Describe the before, the trigger and the after. Mention his changed view of both books and teacher.
questions.commonMistake: Listing his feelings without showing the change from one state to another.

questions.prompt: Write a character sketch of M. Hamel, using evidence from the story.
questions.answer: M. Hamel is a dedicated teacher who has served the village for many years. He is normally strict and impatient, but on the last day he is gentle with Franz and does not scold him. His best clothes show his respect for the occasion and for his pupils. He is honest: he blames himself as well as the pupils and their parents for neglected learning. He is deeply patriotic, praising French and urging people to protect it. His emotion at the end, when he cannot speak and writes Vive la France on the blackboard, shows how much he loves both his country and his work. He is therefore a strict but caring man of dignity.
questions.explanation: Give four or five qualities, each backed with an action. Include his strictness and his change of manner.
questions.commonMistake: Describing him only as strict. The last day reveals his gentler and more patriotic side.

questions.prompt: M. Hamel says that people often put off learning until tomorrow. Do you think the story is only about French, or does it apply to every learner? Give reasons.
questions.answer: The story is set around one language, but its message applies to every learner. Franz, the parents and even the teacher had all assumed there would always be another day. When the chance disappears, they see its value too late. This is true of any subject or skill: students who postpone study often regret it when an examination or an opportunity arrives. At the same time, the story has a particular historical meaning, since language is being taken away by force. So a balanced answer says the story has two layers: a specific one about identity and a universal one about not delaying what matters.
questions.explanation: Marks are for a clear view, reference to the postponement theme, and a link to the learner's own life.
questions.commonMistake: Repeating the plot without discussing the wider lesson.

questions.prompt: Why do you think the story is told by a child rather than by the teacher or a villager? What effect does this choice have?
questions.answer: A child narrator lets the reader discover the situation as Franz does, slowly, through small clues such as the silence, the clothes and the villagers. His innocence makes the sadness stronger because he begins by thinking only of playing and being scolded, and later understands the seriousness of the loss. A teacher or an adult might have explained the politics directly and made the story less emotional. The child's changing feelings also make the theme of regret easier to feel.
questions.explanation: Talk about the gradual discovery, the innocence of the narrator and the added emotion.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that the narrator is a boy, without explaining the effect on the reader.
